title: Appendix A. Primary-source reading map
html:
Appendix A. Primary-source reading map

This index separates the surviving ancient sources from later interpretations. A passage's presence establishes what its author reports; it does not independently verify every event described. Read parallel Gospel accounts separately before combining them. Matthew and Luke reuse Mark, and Luke-Acts forms one author's two-volume narrative, so repeated material is not automatically independent corroboration.

New Testament

The table covers the principal narrative units and retrospective references to the Baptist. Ranges sometimes include surrounding context. The linked entries provide convenient starting points; the book-and-verse references identify the remaining passages in any complete Bible.

Source Passages What the passages contribute
Mark, beginning with chapter 1S12 1:2-11, 14; 2:18-22 John's preaching, appearance, baptism of Jesus, imprisonment; his disciples' fasting.
Mark 6:14-29; 8:27-28; 9:11-13 Execution and burial; speculation that Jesus is John returned; Elijah and suffering.
Mark 11:27-33 Jesus challenges opponents to explain the authority behind John's baptism.
Source Passages What the passages contribute
Matthew, beginning with chapter 3S79 3:1-17; 4:12; 9:14-17 Repentance, judgment, Abrahamic ancestry, John's objection to baptizing Jesus, arrest, fasting.
Matthew 11:2-19; 14:1-12 John's prison question, Jesus's praise, Elijah identification, criticisms of asceticism, death.
Matthew 16:13-14; 17:10-13; 21:23-27, 32 John's public reputation, Elijah, baptismal authority, reception by tax collectors and prostitutes.
Luke, beginning with chapter 1S80 1:5-25, 36-80; 3:1-22 Parents, annunciation, birth, childhood; ministry's chronological setting, ethical instructions, imprisonment, Jesus's baptism.
Luke 5:33-39; 7:18-35; 9:7-9, 18-19 Fasting and prayer, prison inquiry, praise and rejection, Herod's and the crowd's speculation.
Luke 11:1; 16:16; 20:1-8 John taught prayer; his place in salvation history; baptism's authority.
John, beginning with chapter 1S25 1:6-8, 15, 19-42 Witness to Jesus; denials of messianic/Elijah identity; Spirit testimony; disciples move toward Jesus.
John 3:22-36; 4:1-3; 5:31-36; 10:40-42 Overlapping baptizing ministries, concerns about followers, bridegroom image, lamp metaphor, remembered testimony.
Source Passages What the passages contribute
Acts 1:5, 21-22; 10:37; 11:16; 13:24-25 John's baptism as the ministry's starting point; contrast between water and Spirit; retrospective proclamation.
Acts 18-19S81 18:24-28; 19:1-7 Apollos and Ephesian disciples: John's baptism continues to matter after his death.

For the scriptural framework, compare Isaiah 40:3-5; Malachi 3:1 and 4:5-6; and 2 Kings 1:8. These are earlier texts subsequently applied to John. They do not name him. Malachi 4:5-6 corresponds to 3:23-24 in Jewish chapter numbering. In all these readings, distinguish John the Baptist from other New Testament figures named John.

Josephus

Read Josephus, Antiquities 18.116-119, corresponding to Book XVIII, chapter 5, section 2 in Whiston's translationS82. This is the essential non-Christian account: John's moral teaching, immersion, popular influence, Antipas's fear, imprisonment, and death at Machaerus. Read the surrounding chapter for the war with Aretas and Herodian family relationships. Whiston's eighteenth-century explanatory footnotes are not Josephus's own words; some harmonize his narrative with the Gospels.

Qur'an

The principal passages concerning Yaḥyā are Qur'an 3:38-41S83, announcing his birth and prophetic character; 19:1-15S64, recounting Zakariyya's prayer and describing Yaḥyā's wisdom and righteousness; 6:85S63, listing him among righteous figures; and 21:89-90S69, describing the answer to his father's prayer. Later commentaries and prophetic legends expand these notices and should be identified separately.

Early Christian noncanonical index

Gospel of Thomas 46S84: praise of John combined with the

  • claim that becoming little and knowing the kingdom surpasses him. An awkward phrase about eyes has differing translations.

  • Gospel of the Hebrews / Gospel of the Nazarenes: scholarly fragment guideS85: fragments associated with Jerome discuss Jesus's need for baptism and the Spirit resting upon him. Their assignment among separate Jewish-Christian gospels is disputed; no complete text survives. Gospel of the Ebionites: fragments and source guideS86:

  • excerpts preserved by Epiphanius alter John's diet and expand Jesus's baptism. They illuminate later vegetarian and theological interpretations. Protevangelium of James 22-24S87: Elizabeth and John

  • escape Herod through a miraculously opened mountain; Zechariah is murdered. These stories are absent from Luke. Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions 1.54 and 1.60S88: depicts

  • followers claiming John is the Christ. This is later controversial literature, not a contemporary transcript.
